lidocaine.name: Lidocain (Lignocain)
notes: Most commonly used for infiltration, peripheral nerve blocks, IV regional
Safer than bupivacaine in cardiac toxicity (CC:CNS ratio ~ 7)
Acts on sodium channels reversibly; does not accumulate in cardiac tissue
Use with epinephrine unless contraindicated (finger/toe/penis/nose tip)

bupivacaine.name: Bupivacain
bupivacaine.onset: 5–10 phút (gây tê ngoài màng cứng); 15–30 phút (phong bế ngoại vi)
notes: Preferred for long-duration blocks and spinal anaesthesia
⚠ Cardiotoxic — avoid intravascular injection. CC:CNS ratio ~ 2
Levobupivacaine (S-enantiomer) has ~30% less cardiotoxicity
Never use 0.75% for obstetric epidural (FDA warning)
Intralipid must be available

levobupivacaine.name: Levobupivacain
notes: Less cardiotoxic than racemic bupivacaine
Equivalent efficacy to bupivacaine
Commonly used for continuous peripheral nerve blocks

ropivacaine.name: Ropivacain
notes: Less motor block than bupivacaine at equianalgesic doses
Preferred for continuous infusions (less tachyphylaxis, more sensory-selective)
⚠ Off-label for spinal anaesthesia in most countries

mepivacaine.name: Mepivacain
notes: Intermediate duration
Often used for peripheral blocks where faster recovery needed
Poor in neonates (reduced metabolism)

prilocaine.name: Prilocain
notes: Good for IV regional anaesthesia (Bier block)
⚠ Doses > 600 mg risk methaemoglobinaemia
Avoid in pregnancy, infants < 6 months

chloroprocaine.name: 2-Chloroprocain
notes: Rapidly metabolised by plasma cholinesterase — ideal for pregnancy
Ester → risk of allergy (PABA metabolite)
Useful for emergency CS top-up through existing epidural
